candidates.bio: R. Shmuel b. Nachmani was a student of R. Yochanan who became an influential scholar often sent by the Sanhedrin to Babylonia. He was known for his colorful homiletics and his longevity.

Like many others, R. Shmuel b. Yitzchak left Babylonia to study in Israel. As he established himself there, he became close to his teacher, R. Chiyya - to the point that he mourned the latter's death as would have a family member; something repeated by his devoted student, Rav Zera, when he died. He was particularly known for his kindness in helping brides rejoice at their weddings.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani was an Eretz Yisraeli Amora of the second and third generations, active in the 3rd and 4th centuries, who resided primarily in Lod. A kohen, he was among the greatest Jewish aggadists. He studied under Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and also saw the Tanna Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar; his colleague was Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi. Though he engaged extensively in halakha and was considered a leading authority of his generation, he was especially renowned for aggadah, earning the title "ba'al aggadah." Many of his aggadic teachings were quoted by Rabbi Chelbo. His sons included the Amora Rabbi Hillel ben Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and Nachman.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak was a third-generation Amora born in Babylonia who ascended to Eretz Yisrael. He was considered, together with Rabbi Zeira, the greatest sage of his generation in Eretz Yisrael, and was known primarily as an aggadist.

Rav Shmuel b. Rav Avahu was a Jewish sage of the second generation of Savoraim, on the border of the first generation. He was the son of Rav Avahu, a sage of Pumbedita in the late Amoraic period. His colleague and disputant was Rav Achai, and they appear together in two sugyot in the Babylonian Talmud.
Rav Shmuel b. Yehuda was a third-generation Babylonian Amora who later immigrated to Eretz Yisrael.

Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat was a first- and second-generation Babylonian Amora and a student of Rav. All halakhot he cites in the Talmud are transmitted in Rav's name. He was renowned as a dedicated teacher of young children; the Talmud records that he taught uninterrupted for thirteen years, earning Rav's praise with the verse from Daniel 12:3. Rav entrusted him with pedagogical guidance and requested that he deliver his eulogy so as to warm the hearts of listeners and bring them to tears. He was a wealthy man. A tradition identifies him as a descendant of Haman who studied Torah in Bnei Brak, though the Lubavitcher Rebbe concluded that his primary residence was Babylonia, with occasional study and teaching in Eretz Yisrael. His son was the Amora Rav Yehuda b. Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat.
R. Shmuel was a student of R. Abahu and of R. Zeira and a fourth generation talmudic sage of the Land of israel.

The prophet Samuel (Shmuel in Hebrew) led the Israelites before the King Saul, the first king, was anointed. Under his leadership, Israel rose up against the Phillistines. He anointed Saul as king and advised him before secretly anointing David when God decided Saul was no longer fit to be king.

Shmuel also left his native Babylonia to study at Rabbi's academy. Coming back before Rav and outliving him, Shmuel established Neharedea as the leading center of Torah study in Babylonia. Besides his Torah scholarship, Shmuel was famous for being an astronomer and physician and was honored by King Shapur I of Persia.

Shmuel the Little was a scholar known for his great humility and concern for others. Hence he was chosen to compose the text of a blessing (in the Amidah prayer) calling for the elimination of those endangering the Jewish people.
